utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, counsel, for the Prosecution, Ekkehard Withopf, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to everyone, the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and all the staff of this courtroom. The witness envisaged for yesterday could not be freed of his obligations, and we will continue his hearing today with the cross-examination. And after that, we will also have two other witnesses who have been planned for today. I'm going to ask the usher to be kind enough to bring our witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. We are continuing today your testimony. You will have to answer questions from the lawyers of the accused, as the examination-in-chief ended yesterday. Should you have any difficulties or should you not feel well, you will let me know and we will immediately interrupt the hearing to allow you time to rest. I hope you are well for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Everything is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now call on the Defence and give them the floor for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Judge, good morning Your Honours, good morning Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kegelj. My name is Stefane Bourgon, and together with my colleagues, Ms. Residovic and Ms. Milanovic, we represent the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic. I only have a few questions for you this morning, knowing that this testimony may be painful for you. I should like to confirm, Mr. Kegelj, that Dusina is indeed in the Zenica municipality and that though your unit was not a member of the Jure Francetic Brigade, it had its headquarters there, but your unit reported to the HVO command in Busovaca. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But Dusina is about 20 kilometres from Zenica, and four to five kilometres from Busovaca, so that we were much closer to Busovaca than to Zenica. Now, who determined this, I don't know why we belonged to Busovaca and not Zenica. Probably because of the distance. Twenty kilometres to Zenica and only four or five kilometres to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. Can you also confirm that before the events in Dusina, the conflict broke out between the HVO and the BH army in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A day or two prior to that. I don't know exactly, but the conflict started in Busovaca two or three days earlier. We remained quiet. We remained in the village. We had no orders. We stayed in the village. We just guarded our own houses. We kept guard duty around our houses, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. Your commander at the time in the area of Dusina was Franjo Rajic, whereas the HVO commander was Dragan Rados, the commander at Brdo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Kegelj, that on the 25th of January, 1993, the HVO attacked the village of Merdani, and you could hear artillery fire as far as Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some shooting, but who attacked who, I don't know. I just heard the shooting that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That evening, the night between the 25th and the 26th of January, you and other HVO soldiers slept in a Serb house situated in the centre of the Croatian part of Dusina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We were -- kept guard duty until midnight. Then usually after midnight we would rest. Everything was peaceful around the village, even though two or three days prior to that, many soldiers had been noticed in the Muslim village, and in the lower part of Dusina village, large groups of soldiers had been noticed. But Zvonko Rajic said that everything had been arranged, that nothing would happen, and that is how we were at rest, and after midnight we all fell asleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. And on the morning of the 26th of January, when you surrendered to the forces of the BH army, it was at that moment that you noticed that Blasko Bosnjak left before you and that he was wounded; he came out before you and he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was awakened by the noise of shooting, and before that, when we ran out of the house, Blasko Bosnjak was lying wounded on the snow. Then he cried out: Flee from here. He said that he had been hit by a sniper from the area of Dusina, from a hill known as Tuleg [phoen]. From that hill, in the Muslim part of the village, a sniper had hit him in the leg. And there was this open, exposed area in front of the house, so we quickly fled to the garage or the basement. At the same time we helped him, we pulled him into the garage as well. We brought a blanket, wrapped him in it, and that is where we remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was following those events, Mr. Kegelj, that you were allowed to take a stretcher to transport him to the Muslim part of the village, where there were some medical personnel to treat him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we surrendered, they searched us. We handed over our weapons. And then we were ordered, and there were four of us, plus Blasko Bosnjak, the wounded man as the fifth. We said that we had a wounded man. They brought a stretcher for us and they ordered two of us, as I and Mladen Kegelj were up front, we were ordered to carry him. And they ordered us to run as fast as we could. So that they beat us all the time. And I received quite a number of blows, because this was a distance of some 700 to 800 metres that we had to cover at a running pace and carrying him at the same time. We carried him to the centre of the village, where there was the medical staff. We left him there. Other soldiers carried him inside, and I didn't see anything after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. You also know that when you surrendered, Drazen Kegelj and Franjo Rajic fled in another direction and that the two were killed that day during the conflict. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we ran out of the house, I can't remember. Some stayed there. Others, Franjo Rajic, said that he was going to help the civilians. And I don't know anything about that. He left us, and I don't know how he was killed. What happened after that, I don't know, as far as he's concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, when you surrendered, you didn't know how the conflict in Dusina had started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I woke up, and when I ran outside, I saw strong forces already entering the upper part of the Croatian village. From the other side, from Hrastovo Kosa, I also saw troops approaching, only they were at some distance. Below our village, there was a grouping of forces also that were not approaching but were there. From the eastern side, from the direction of the village of Dusina, I just saw troops in the village. I saw soldiers moving around the village. So that from the direction of the north, I did see strong forces attacking, who were chasing out civilians, civilians were moving towards Stipe Kegelj's house already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. When, a little later, you came to the crossroads, you met a man who you described as Edin Hakanovic. You know that Mr. Edin Hakanovic, before the conflict, was a civilian policeman in Visoko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Edin Hakanovic after we had handed over the wounded man. We were mistreated there. We were forced to be barefoot on the snow for 15 to 20 minutes, maybe up to half an hour. Then we were taken back to the area between the Muslim and Croatian part of the village. In Potok, I saw Edin Hakanovic, when we joined the civilians, the four of us and the civilians who had also been brought there to the centre. I saw Edin Hakanovic then, and he said: No harm will come to you. I took over -- I took charge of this operation voluntarily, and nothing can happen to you. I'm responsible for everything. Just then, someone said to my aunt that her 19-year-old son had been killed in front of my house. She cried out and fainted, and then the soldiers -- I heard bursts of fire to keep us quiet, to prevent us from shouting and panicking. Then Edin Hakanovic said what he said, and he escorted us, together with a group of soldiers, as far as the village of Brdo, where we were used as a human shield, and he said that we were going there for the other HVO soldiers to surrender. So he went with us to the village of Brdo and then he brought us back to Stipe's house. After that, I didn't see Edin Hakanovic again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. Are you aware, Mr. Kegelj, that there's a trial in Zenica against Edin Hakanovic, who is charged for events linked to the events in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. As I'm living in the USA, in America, I'm not aware of what is going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. Yesterday you testified at length about the experiences you had. I certainly have no intention of asking you to repeat the painful experiences of your life, but nevertheless, when those events were over, this person Geler threatened you and said if you spoke to anyone, you would be given special treatment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Probably as I survived, Geler ordered me not to tell anyone about it, because otherwise he will settle accounts with me in a special manner, should I tell anyone or should anyone notice on me the effects of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, it is following those events that you were taken to the Muslim part of the village, and then another group of soldiers took you again to the school in Lasva. And there, can you confirm that soldiers were put in one room and the civilians in another room? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When I arrived there, HVO soldiers of Lasva, Visnjica -- Lasva and Visnjica were already in one classroom. I was immediately put there with them. There were three of us: Myself, Milenko Rajic, Franjo Rajic. And they told Franjo Rajic then, as he was a civilian, he was moved to the other classroom where the civilians were, next to ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible, Mr. Kegelj, that you're really talking about Franjo Kristo, not Franjo Rajic, that you've confused the names?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I mixed the two up. I confused the names. It's Franjo Kristo. That's right. Franjo Rajic was killed on the 26th, in the morning. I said, I, Milenko Rajic, and Franjo Kristo. That is quite right. That is correct. I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were in the school, you were allowed to see your wife and your two children and the only person you spoke to about the unfortunate events that happened in Dusina was your wife; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. My wife wanted to visit me. I didn't know what had happened to my wife and my children. I was taken to the classroom first, and maybe about 15 minutes or half an hour later, civilians were also taken to Lasva, to the school. At that point, my wife asked permission to visit me. The guards who were guarding us allowed me to go out among the civilians and to spend a few minutes with my wife. I was with her for 10 to 15 minutes. During that time, as I didn't know what was going to happen to me, and as I could no longer see Geler there, I briefly told my wife about what had happened and told her that perhaps if I died, she'd be able to tell people what had happened. I wanted her to know what had happened to the other people at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kegelj, yesterday, in response to a question from my learned colleague, you said that all the soldiers, about 1.00 in the morning, were transported to the KP Dom. Is it correct that you spent three days in the KP Dom, in the penal and correctional facility, before you were exchanged? I apologise, Mr. Kegelj. Perhaps there's a translation error. I can see that in the transcript, it says three days. My question was 13 days. Is it correct that after you had spent 13 days in the KP Dom, you were exchanged, and you then went to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I spent 13 days in the KP Dom, and on the 13th day we were exchanged. After about a week in the KP Dom in Zenica, we were visited by UNPROFOR. They took down our details. They registered us as prisoners. We were then all given three possibilities: To go to Zenica, to go to Vitez, or to Busovaca. Those were the three possibilities I had. I chose to go to Busovaca. However, they all chose to go either to Vitez or Busovaca. No one went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. And perhaps my last question. Following the events in Busovaca you didn't speak to anyone about the events until you met representatives of the OTP in February 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. As soon as I got to Busovaca, some HVO representatives -- in fact, I don't know who they were. They were in Busovaca, though, and I then gave statements to two persons in Busovaca. That was two or three months afterwards. That's when I gave statements. And then I gave a statement two years ago, or two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. I have the statement. We have the statement that you gave in Busovaca. My question was: Between Busovaca and the time when you met investigators from the OTP. That's the period that I was referring to. Thank you for answering my questions, Mr. Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The other Defence team told me yesterday that they didn't have any questions for the witness. I'm turning to the Prosecution. No questions, Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Thank you. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution just has one or perhaps two questions that arise from the cross-examination. Re-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you responded that when you were in the Lasva school, you were allowed to see your wife because, as you put it: I could no longer see Geler there." Did you see this person Geler at the Lasva elementary school during the period that you were there on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there. The last time I saw him was when we took the dead men to the cellar. We returned to Stipe Kegelj's house. And when we had been taken out of Stipe Kegelj's house, once we'd been taken to the school -- well, the last time was in Stipe Kegelj's house. That's the last time I saw him. I never saw Geler after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, for your testimony that you gave yesterday and that you have given today. We know that the events that you have spoken about have reminded you of unpleasant experiences. The Defence took care to ask you questions about these events, questions that were of a general nature. You have contributed to determining the truth. We would like to thank you and we wish you a good trip home to the USA. I'm now going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to the Prosecution for information about the witness. Mr. Withopf, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, there are two further witnesses scheduled for today, namely, Mr. Jozo Erenda and Mr. Alija Podrug. Jozo Erenda will be available by 10.00. For this reason, I am not sure whether the witness is already available now or whether he is on his way. If I may please ask the usher to check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have any protective measures been requested or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, none of the two witnesses will request protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The question, then, is: Is the witness here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has told me that he will be here in a quarter of an hour. So we'll have a 15-minute break and we will resume as soon as the witness arrives. --- Break taken at 9.31 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Could the usher go and call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying into your own language. Can you hear what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution, you must make a solemn declaration. Before you do so, you should tell me your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jozo Erenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 16th of September, 1953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Cukle, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Cukle, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently unemployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your usual profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked as a tradesman and as an official, as a clerk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In 1993, what was your profession? That's over ten years ago. What did you do at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was an accountant in the Putnik company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before a Tribunal or is this the first time that you have come to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where have you already testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1977, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will now make a solemn declaration. I'm going to ask the usher to show you the text, which you should read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. now. Before the Prosecution commences its examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you some information to ensure the proceedings run smoothly. You will have to first have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. They are sitting to your right. They will be asking you some questions that you will have to answer. To the extent that this is possible, try to provide precise answers to the questions. Once the examination-in-chief has been concluded, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will also ask you a series of questions. Depending on the type of questions put to you, try to answer the questions correctly. If you don't understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. If you encounter any difficulties, let us know. In addition, the three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions. At any time they think it is necessary, and they will do this in the light of the questions put to you by either of the parties. If the Judges feel that it's necessary to clarify anything, the Judges will ask you questions to do so. As you have also sworn to tell the truth, you should not lie, because if you give false testimony, you could be prosecuted, and the penalties, according to our Rules, could be either a fine or a prison sentence of up to seven years. In addition, if, when answering a question, you provide information that could be used to subsequently prosecute you, if you provide information that might incriminate you, in such a case, you can refuse to answer the question. But the Trial Chamber can force you to answer the question. However, if that is the case, the answer you provide can't be used against you. I have just provided you with an outline of the way in which these proceedings will be conducted. Without wasting any more time, I'll now turn to the Prosecution, who may proceed. I think Ms. Benjamin will be conducting the examination-in-chief. Good day, Mrs. Ben.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. First I wish to apologise to the Trial Chamber and to my colleagues and to the witness for the little misunderstanding that took place just now. Examined by Ms. Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Erenda.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated -- you have indicated to the Trial Chamber where you were born and the municipality in which Cukle was situated. Could you tell the Trial Chamber the ethnic composition of Cukle, please, at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: The ratio was 65:35. The Croats were in the majority, but this data is not quite precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated to us that you appeared in a trial in 1977. Could you tell the Trial Chamber in what capacity you appeared in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I was the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you convicted?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. I was given a three-year sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve your sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since then, and up until the present, have you had any other problems with the law?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you state for the Trial Chamber, please, if you did national service, compulsory national service, with the JNA, and for how long, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I did my military service in the JNA, from the 27th of October, 1972 until the 25th of January, 1974, in Zabok, in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your service with the JNA, did there come a time when you would have joined any other army or any other unit, military body?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. Having been expelled from the village of Cukle when the conflict was ongoing, I joined the HVO Vitez Brigade in Stara Bila, it's part of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect to your observations, could you tell us, in relation to around April of 1993, if you observed that there was a change in the village of Cukle.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. Changes could be noticed in the village of Cukle and the village of Pode. Between these two villages there are Muslim inhabitants, on a hill between those two villages; BH army troops went there. That's the sort of flag they were carrying. They took up position there, but they didn't relocate at that time in Travnik in 1993. There was some tension. But after the May holidays, when there was a massacre in Mulatici [phoen] village, they related to inhabitants from Cukle and then there was some tension. So in the evening we placed the inhabitants in three houses and we stood village guard. But during the day, we would till the land, because that was the period for farming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said that a flag was placed. Would you be able to tell us if you were able to recognise this flag and to whom it belonged?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised the flag, because, as the crow flies, it may be some 200 metres from my house. It was on a large pole and it was a big flag, and I recognised it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you were shown this flag today or a picture of this flag, would you be able to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Trial Chamber's permission, may the witness be shown Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P4, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is number 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to you, number 12 would be the flag that you saw placed in the village of Cukle around April?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Around the 18th or the 20th. I can't be more precise about the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us, if you are aware, by whom was this flag placed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the person individually, but I know that there were Muslims in that area and with that flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Much obliged. Now, Mr. Erenda, could you relate to the Trial Chamber your experience on the 8th of June, 1993, at the commencement of the conflict, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: In the morning, on the 8th of June, about 4.30 a.m., the village of Cukle was attacked. The hamlet of Mrkonje, and behind that hamlet are Muslim settlements, Vode [phoen] Mehurici, and Vranici. House started to be set on fire and we rounded up the population and started withdrawing. They were shooting. Houses were set on fire. And we withdrew with the population. During the process, people were wounded and there were people sick. We went towards Ovnak, Grahovcici, and Cehine Kuce, and we stayed there until about 2100 and 2200 hours and then we continued on our way to Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erenda, you have indicated to the Trial Chamber that they were shooting, houses were burning. Could you explain for us whom you mean when you say "they."

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. Who were burning? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Who was doing the burning? Who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: That army. There were a lot of them, in fact. One could hear a lot of noise, a lot of shooting and cries: "Allah U Ekber" and "Tek bir." So it was the Muslim army, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, if you can, what was the ethnic background of the owners of these houses that you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: It was the Croat houses that were burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that for some 22 hours, you travelled from Cukle and finally to Nova Bila. Did you remain in Nova Bila for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Nova Bila and Stara Bila are close by. Some left Nova Bila and went to Vitez, Busovaca, and Novi Travnik, but I remained in Stara Bila, which is right next to Nova Bila, and I stayed there until I returned to Cukle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to go back to your house in Cukle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. I returned in 2001, in the month of May. I went to someone else's house and I tilled the land and I was given some building material. So I built a house and moved into it last year, on the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But after the conflict, your house, was it standing when you went back to Cukle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: No. It had been totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call on the Defence to start their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Erenda. My name is Edina Residovic. I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. Will you be kind enough to answer some questions put by me, as you have done in answering questions by my friend from the Prosecution. You said that you were born and that you grew up in the village of Cukle, which is within Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Cukle is divided into Gornje and Donje Cukle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The population of the whole village of Cukle was mixed, both Croats and Muslims lived there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, most Muslims lived in Gornje Cukle. The Muslim houses were actually in the middle, whereas Croat houses were around Gornje Cukle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around the village of Cukle, there were other Croat villages, Ovnak, Susanj, Grahovcici, and Novo Selo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To explain better the position of your village for the benefit of Their Honours in particular, is it true that Gornje Cukle is about two to three kilometres from Ovnak, four to five kilometres from Grahovcici, about seven kilometres from Guca Gora, Maljine, and Mehurici? Roughly, would that roughly be the distances between your village and these other villages?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Guca Gora is further away, quite a bit further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the distance is?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: About ten kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mehurici and Maljine are still further away, by another two kilometres; is that right, from Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: In relation to Cukle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Is it true, Mr. Erenda, that in 1993 you were aware of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina had become an internationally recognised state?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. We had voted for a unified, indivisible country, both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew that it was a member of the UN at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I really don't know much about politics, but perhaps that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the legitimate armed force of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: The army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time was the legitimate armed force of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You knew that; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Well, let it be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are also aware that to go from Zenica to Travnik, you had to go through the pass Ovnak or Novo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew that in the spring, especially as of April 1993, at Ovnak, the HVO had its checkpoint, and fortified [Realtime transcript read in error "45"] lines from Ovnak towards Grahovcici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I don't remember, because we didn't really leave Cukle much. We didn't leave the village much, and we had very little contact with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. There seems to be something in the transcript, probably due to an error in the translation. It says 45 lines, and I said: In April or May, there were fortified lines between Ovnak and Grahovcici. And the witness said that he's not well aware of that because he didn't leave Cukle. So it's an error in the interpretation. Thank you. I had to draw your attention to the error in the transcript. You also know that the HVO, in April 1993, proclaimed a general mobilisation and mobilised all able-bodied men in your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Everyone wasn't mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also know that there were sporadic clashes at the checkpoint at Ovnak because HVO members who manned this checkpoint would stop members of the army who were going to the front lines against the Serbs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in Grahovcici, a part of the Frankopan Brigade was stationed and that those units were joined by a significant number of soldiers from the Jure Francetic Brigade. When that brigade was disarmed in Zenica in the second half of April? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you recognised the symbol under 12. It was the regular army of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The regular flag. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that as of April the HVO ceased going to the front lines against the Serbs, but rather, men started holding guard duty around their villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I don't know about any HVO units, but we in Cukle did keep guard duty in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also dug trenches facing the Muslim villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said in answer to questions from my learned friend, Croats and Muslims in the village of Cukle were not in conflict right up until the end of May 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: In Cukle, there were no tensions between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answering a question from the Prosecution, you said that the tension started around the 1st of May, after you had heard that five men had been killed in Miletici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, prior to that, you heard of the massacre in the village of Ahmici, where more than a hundred inhabitants of that village had been killed, and that event created certain fears among the Croats, fears of revenge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, your neighbours, Muslims, those belonging to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, did not demonstrate any wish to take their revenge on their neighbours in the village of Cukle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: There were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please: How far from Cukle is Postinje and Mrkonje?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: There is no Mrkonje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Postinje?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Postinje, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it from Cukle? A moment ago we gave the distances to Maljine, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Postinje is closer than Guca Gora by about three kilometres. It is on the other side of the Bila River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mrkonje?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Mrkonje is a component part of Cukle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my mistake in mentioning Mokrinje [phoen] instead of this area of Cukle. You said that you were keeping guard duty in the village on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard the shooting, you didn't really know who was doing the shooting, nor could you see just then any insignia on the units who were shooting around the village then?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: I didn't see insignia, nor did I recognise any faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About an hour later, as you said, together with other members of the HVO, you started withdrawing towards Nova Bila, but you first went towards Ovnak and Grahovcici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went in that direction because you knew that HVO forces there were stronger and that they were quite well dug in?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: We had no choice. We couldn't go to Han Bila because that area is inhabited by Muslims as well. So this was the only route that could lead to some sort of salvation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was only when you arrived in Grahovcici where HVO members and civilians from other villages were gathering, it was only then that you were able to see at the front lines around Gornje Cukle that there was smoke, which meant that some houses had been set on fire in the course of the fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, at the time, you didn't know how these houses had been set on fire and you didn't know who had done that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Gornje Cukle, the first time you returned there was in 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was only then that you could see the extent to which the houses in Cukle had been damaged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, you also didn't know who had set fire to certain houses in Cukle. You did not know how, and under what circumstances, and you didn't know who had looted these houses?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, some inhabitants of Cukle returning to their village after repairs had been carried out on the houses?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Relations with the neighbours are normal?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims built my house. I was provided with some material and then I paid the workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Neighbours helping each other to return to a normal sort of life?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erenda. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't think that the other Defence team has any questions. The Trial Chamber would like to ask you a minor question following the answer you have just provided. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1996 you returned to your village and you saw that your house had been burnt down. Had the house been completely destroyed? What could you actually see?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: My house had been mined. It had been completely destroyed, so I had to use a bulldozer to clear the area. It had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, you said that your house had been destroyed, a bomb had been planted, it exploded, and it destroyed the house. So your house was destroyed as a result of the explosive device that had been planted there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: When we were withdrawing, I noticed that it was on fire. But when I returned there -- well, it had been destroyed. Its foundations. I assume that an explosive device had been planted there, because I doubt that if it had only been set on fire, the damage wouldn't have been that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you had the house rebuilt and you used a bulldozer to do this, there was no property remaining in the house, a fridge, a television, a radio? Everything had been taken, or did you find any of your property there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ERENDA
utterances.text: Some things had been taken away. I found the bath there and a few other items, but not many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Prosecution have any additional questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no re-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, this concludes your examination. You have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution and by the Defence. We thank you for having contributed to determining what happened. Thank you, and now I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. We wish you a good trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning to the Prosecution to ask them about the third witness. Mr. Withopf, what can you tell us about the third witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the third witness is available. I may, however, suggest to take the regular break now, which would allow my colleague, Mr. Chester Stamp, to come down and to commence with the witness after the break. It can be anticipated that the third witness can be completed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As we had a 15-minute break a minute ago, we'll have a 20- to 25-minute break now. We'll resume at 10 to 11.00 or 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. The Trial Chamber would like to greet Mr. Stamp. Could the usher bring our witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask, before the usher does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There's one matter we wish to address Your Honours about, the scope of the testimony of this witness. And we thought it would be more efficient to do it before the witness comes into the Court, so that his testimony isn't potentially interrupted and there are long discussions with the witness present in Court. We are concerned about a certain part of the testimony of this witness. He addresses many topics in his statement. I don't know if Your Honours have a copy of his statement to hand. But one of the main topics of his testimony is his arrest and detention in various detention facilities, including the Music School. Your Honour may be aware, but this witness is not a person of Bosnian Croat or Bosnian Serb extraction. He is a Bosniak, in particular, a Bosnian Muslim, who was associated in the past with the Bosnian army. Our concern is that in the indictment, nowhere is it alleged that the accused are responsible under Article 7(3) for the alleged detention of Bosniak citizens. The indictment simply alleges, in paragraphs 41 and 42, that the persons imprisoned and detained were Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs. There's no allegation that any Bosnian Muslims were detained and that the accused are charged with their detention. In addition, Your Honour, in the pre-trial brief, at paragraphs 81 to 84, in connection with -- this is the Music School, one of the alleged detention facilities, the Prosecution again states that the accused were on notice that Croat and Serbs prisoners were held at the Music School. That's paragraph 81 in particular, Your Honours. The Prosecution may well respond that they are calling this witness in order to show the kinds of activities at these detention facilities or the pattern of alleged violence at these facilities. In our submission, it would be prejudicial to allow the witness to testify about such matters, firstly because the Prosecution is able to and has already led evidence with regard to the detention of Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Serb persons at, in particular, the Music School. And in our submission, it would be prejudicial to use this kind of evidence as a supplement to the evidence that has already been heard by Your Honours. In addition to that, Your Honours, the witness cannot, looking at his statement, it may be that there's more beyond his statement, but he cannot testify about matters relating to the treatment of Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Serb persons at the Music School. There's also potentially a difficult legal matter involved, Your Honour, in that Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions arguably only applies to persons who are on different sides of the conflict, that the victim and the perpetrator are linked to different sides, but might not apply in situations where you are looking at the armed forces dealing with their own persons. And it's another factor to be taken into account to show why this is a separate case to those that we have already heard. It's for all of those reasons, Your Honour, that we wish to request Your Honours to limit the scope of the testimony of this witness to those topics which do not concern his arrest and detention, as this is a matter not charged in the indictment, and, in our submission, although Your Honours are able to hear evidence and exclude it later, our request is that it is excluded now, because it would be prejudicial for Your Honours to hear such evidence and for the public to hear such evidence when, in fact, this is evidence that cannot be used against our clients in proving the charges in the indictment. And it's for those reasons that we wish to try and, before the witness testifies, constrain the limits of his testimony. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dixon. We've taken note of your comments. I'm going to let the Prosecution address the issue now. But to summarise what you have said: You pointed out that the witness was detained in the detention facility, but that he did not belong to the category of victims referred to in the indictment. In -- the indictment mentions victims of Serb or Croat ethnicity, whereas in this case, the witness is a Bosniak. You have also pointed out that, given that this witness was not a victim, he can't be included within the scope. Scope of the questions has to be limited. That is what you have claimed. The Prosecution will inform us of its position. As you know, there are a number of different types of witnesses. We have expert witnesses, we have victims, and then we have simple, ordinary witnesses. He could be classified as a witness who should not be considered as a victim, in terms of the indictment, and his testimony will be testimony as a -- such as the testimony given by a guard of a detention facility, an international monitor, et cetera. But I would appreciate it if the observation [as interpreted] could state its position with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May it please you. It is -- my friend's submission is something in the nature of a very interesting pre-emptive strike, which is, I understand, a doctrine in international law which is being postulated very vigorously from some quarters. However, even within the submission, I think it contains the seeds of the answer. He said I think that we may refer to it as evidence of a pattern of conduct, and it is evidence of a pattern of conduct, which can be given not only by victims referred to in the indictment, but anybody who suffered the pattern of conduct that has been charged. And I think the Rules of Procedure and Evidence makes specific reference, the receipt of that type of evidence, in Rule 93, where it permits a Court to receive, in the interests of justice, evidence of a pattern. Secondly, the witness and the Court is entitled to hear what the witness has to say about who were the persons who were in charge of the Music School involved in beatings. It is relevant to the matters which the Court will have to adjudicate upon. And again, within the submission my friend has sown the seeds of the answer to his own submission, and that is, these are matters which are relevant and the Court, at the end of the case, at the end of the day, is entitled to give it whatever weight it can. It really ought to hear the evidence before it determines what the probative value is. So notwithstanding that the indictment does not refer to the cruel treatment of Croat by Croat -- sorry - of Bosnian by Bosnian, a Bosnian might well have been in a position to observe events which are relevant to the indictment. This Bosnian clearly was in a position to observe matters which are relevant to the indictment and clearly, it is my submission, respectfully, ought to be heard by the Court. And in due course, at the proper time, the Court ought to give it whatever weight the Court thinks that it deserves. Those are my submissions. May it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, a short reply. I'm not asking that the witness not be heard, but simply that he is not permitted to testify about what happened to him, because he may not be a person protected by the law in that situation. But more importantly, what happened to him is not charged in the indictment. He can give evidence about what he observed from his statement, there's not much that he observed beyond what happened to him, but he can give that evidence. My only request is that he should not be entitled, because this could be prejudicial to the accused, to talk about what occurred to his own personal -- in his own personal situation in the Music School and that that evidence, although the Prosecution is seeking to assert that it can prove a pattern, in my submission, it can't prove a pattern in relation to what happened to Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat persons there, because he's in a separate category. So it can't be used as probative evidence to support such a pattern, and therefore, is irrelevant, worthless to Your Honour's consideration of the facts in this case, and in the interests of justice and the saving of time as well, the Prosecution could be instructed not to ask questions about what happened to the witness himself in the Music School. That is the request that I'm making. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic simply wishes to support the motion submitted by Defence counsel for the accused Kubura regarding Rule 93 of the Rules of Procedure, regarding evidence of consistent pattern of conduct. So this is Rule 93 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is stated there that evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct relevant to serious violations of international humanitarian law under the Statute may be admissible in the interests of justice. We support the motion made by Defence counsel for the accused Kubura to the extent that the facts related to what happened to the witness himself do not come under the scope of Rule 93, and therefore, we support the motion submitted, also relying on Article 3 of the Geneva Convention, that a victim has to be a person on the other side of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will deliberate on this matter. But before we withdraw to deliberate, there are two points that the Chamber would like to learn from the Prosecution. First, the question of Rule 93 and the consistent pattern of conduct. The Chamber would like to know whether this testimony is designed to establish a consistent pattern of conduct. Because if that is the case, then Rule 93(B) refers to Rule 66, and that Rule says that in that case, the Defence needs to be given the evidence and informed of what the Prosecution is relying on to prove this consistent pattern of conduct. And clearly, that procedure has not been observed. A second point: Does the Prosecution wish to ask the witness questions about what he himself experienced, that is, his arrest and conditions of detention and bad treatment? The Defence is saying that that is not covered by the indictment. Or does the Prosecution simply wish to ask the witness about what he saw and what he could say about what happened to others? Then he would be an external witness, but who can certainly testify about facts that took place in his presence. And regarding that type of question, the Defence tells us that they do not object, of course, because he's a simple witness, an ordinary witness, testifying about what he saw, but not about what he himself suffered. Because he doesn't belong to the category of victims in the terms of the indictment. Regarding Rule 93 and the questions planned, I would like to ask the Prosecution to comment. Mr. Stamp, what can you tell us additionally before we deliberate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The submission of the Prosecution in regard to Rule 93 was that a part of the reasons why the evidence ought to be admitted is that it comes within the terms of Rule 93, and I think it is clear from what my learned friend has indicated to the Court that they were served with the documents relevant to this evidence. They were served with the statements indicating what he had to say. So I think that deals with the Rule 66 part of it. Not only are we submitting that the evidence ought to be admitted pursuant to Rule 93, but there are other reasons why it should be admitted. The witness is able to give evidence as to the identity in terms of the units to which the perpetrators belonged. That is something which it is submitted the Court ought to hear and ought not to exclude from the record, and it's really a matter for the Court to ultimately consider as its probative value. The second question which you asked, Mr. President, was as to what exactly we wanted to -- the witness to testify about, whether it is his own experience or what happened to others. It is submitted -- well, before I submit, I will just say it is in regard to his own experience primarily, because his own experience is so inextricably interwoven into what he observed that there would be no point in attempting to sever what he observed from what happened to him, because he observed what he observed as a result of what happened to him. So it cannot be severed. As regards the Common Article 3 issue, I think that has been well settled in the jurisprudence here, and it is an interesting question, but I don't think the question is of much significance in relation to the issue of this witness's testimony. And I have nothing further to add, unless there are any further questions from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to withdraw for a few minutes, and we'll be back shortly. --- Break taken at 11.13 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is going to render its ruling, following an objection made by the Defence counsels regarding the conditions for the testimony of a witness. The Chamber has taken note of the position of the Prosecution as well. The Chamber is of the opinion that there are two problems. One problem linked to Rule 93 and the second problem regarding the scope of the questions put to the witness. Regarding Rule 93 and evidence of consistent pattern of conduct, that there is no reason to consider that questions can be put to the witness to establish a consistent pattern of conduct which, in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief, applies only to Serb or Croatian victims. No mention is made of Bosniak detainees. Therefore, all questions regarding the admissibility of evidence based on relevance cannot be admitted. Therefore, on those grounds, we will not admit as evidence replies by the witness designed to establish a consistent pattern of conduct with respect to Bosniak witnesses. As for the scope of the questions that need to be put to the witness, this witness will only reply to questions regarding what he saw in relation to other co-detainees, and he will not comment on his own position, on his own conditions of detention, nor the reasons which led up to his arrest. His testimony and questions will relate only to what he saw with respect other detainees, who were either Serb or Croat. Under those conditions, and under the control of the Chamber, we shall have the witness brought in. So, Mr. Usher, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stamp. The decision has been rendered. You heard it. The Chamber will not be making any revision of that decision, unless you wish to comment on another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wasn't asking for revision. I was merely asking for a clarification. Will the witness be allowed to testify about the identity of the persons who beat him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have indicated, he will testify about what he saw. His personal condition is not covered by the indictment or the brief. So you will ask him questions about what he saw and not about what happened to him. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Are you receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You will be testifying about events of which you were an eyewitness. Before doing so, you have to make a solemn declaration. But before you make the solemn declaration, you should tell me your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alija Podrug. I was born on the 3rd of February, 1941, in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was your profession in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the chief of security in the Catici power plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before a tribunal, before an International Court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that you will now be testifying, you have to make the solemn declaration. Could you read the text that is before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before the Prosecution takes the floor to conduct its examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the way in which these proceedings will be conducted. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by representatives of the Prosecution. They are to your right. These questions will have to do with the detention facility where you were detained, and you will be asked to answer a certain number of questions. After the Prosecution has concluded its examination-in-chief, you will have to answer questions put to you by the Defence. They will conduct their cross-examination and they will check the truthfulness of your responses, and they will also ask you questions that concern the context that might be relevant for the accused's case. If the three Judges sitting before you feel that it is necessary, they may ask you questions in order to clarify your answers. As you have sworn to tell the truth, you should not lie. If you give false testimony, you could be prosecuted, and the penalty for false testimony could consist of a fine or a prison sentence of up to seven years, or both. In addition, according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, there is a very specific provision which concerns a witness who provides information when answering a question, and this information could be used to prosecute him subsequently. If this is the case, the witness can refuse to answer the question. If the Trial Chamber forces the witness to answer the question, the information that the witness provides can't be used against the witness to prosecute the witness at a subsequent date. It's a little complicated, but I had to inform you of this. We know that you yourself were detained. This was discussed before you entered the courtroom. But it is not your personal situation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that interests the Trial Chamber. It is, in fact, what you saw while you were detained. So this will be the scope of your testimony. You are not considered to be a witness who is a victim in these proceedings. You are considered to be a simple witness, an ordinary witness. I will now turn to Mr. Stamp, who may take the floor. But I would first like to point out to the witness that he should try to answer the questions put to you to him as fully as possible. If you don't understand a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it so that you can understand the question. Sometimes the questions are very complicated and the witness might fail to understand the meaning of a question. If that is the case, you should ask the person putting you the question to rephrase it. If you encounter any difficulties, inform the Trial Chamber of the fact, and we will try to deal with the problem. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Podrug, while you were the manager of Catici -- pardon me. The security manager of Catici in 1993, where was it you were living at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I was expelled from Foca. I arrived in Hrasnica. I reported to my director in Hidrogradnja. I stayed there for a while. He told me to stay on and to work there. I worked there for a certain period of time. I was wounded by a shell. An ambulance then took me to Fojnica, which is where I was treated, and I reported to my director in Hidrogradnja again. He told me to go to Catici, to report to the chief of the construction area and to remain there and to work there. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps there is a translation error, or perhaps there was an error that appeared in the question put by my colleague from the Prosecution. It's at page 40, at the very beginning. A security officer in Catici has been mentioned. I didn't hear the witness mentioning Catici. Could this issue be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Catici shouldn't be confused with the place that he referred to. Could the ask the witness where he was chief of security:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the construction of Hidrogradnja, on the grounds of the Catici power plant. My company, Hidrogradnja, built the power plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to all of this you told us about, you were living in Foca. What was your occupation in Foca?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I also worked for Hidrogradnja, as the chief of security, in Visegrad, the Visegrad construction site, and the headquarters were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, I'm not sure if it's there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in July 1993, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I was living in Hrasnica, and I worked in Butmir, the Hidrogradnja construction site. That's where I was wounded, and the ambulance took me to the hospital in Fojnica. I reported to my head office in Sarajevo. There were communications. The director told me to go to Catici, to report to the chief of the construction site and to stay on there to work. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 27th of July, 1993, at about 8.00, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I was in Visoko, at my relatives' house. I was living there because I couldn't find a flat in Kakanj and I would travel there by -- I would travel to work by ThermoElektrana bus. I was drinking coffee in the yard. A Lada car appeared and there were uniformed young men with beards. They had head bands, green head bands on them with inscriptions in Arabic. I recognised them as members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, because I'd been with the secretary of the brigade, who is from Foca. He's a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the name of the secretary of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Mustafa Oprasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you recognised them as members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Was there any particular reason why you recognised them as such?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Well, I would see them in Kakanj, and they were passing through Catici. And on the grounds of the ThermoElektrana, the power plant where UNPROFOR were located, there were people, women and children of Croatian ethnicity were among the people who were taking refuge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did any of these men who approached you that morning say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: When they arrived, they called someone -- didn't want to say anything. They were armed. They had rifles. They had beards and they had headbands on. They said: "Is your name Alija Podrug?" And I said yes. "Are you the chief of security?" I said yes. They said: "Our commander would like to speak to you." I told them: "I have to go to work now. I'll come later. I know that you're in the Sretno motel. I'll turn up later." They said: "No. Come with us. That's what our commander has told us to do. And come and sit down." When they took me to Kakanj, to the motel, I then said: There's your command --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just stop there a minute. Did the person who spoke to you say who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: They said -- I saw him at Halid Cengic, where I was, in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said? The question was: Did the person who spoke to you say who his commander was? What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: No. He just said the commander. I knew who their commander was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was their commander?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Halil Brzina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also said that you told him that you know -- that you knew that he or they were in the Sretno Motel. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Yes. They told me the commander was in Zenica, and he is waiting for you to be brought there. And that's how they took me off to an unknown place. I didn't know it was the Music School. This is what I found out later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know in any particular unit occupied the Zenica -- sorry - occupied the motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Well, the 7th Muslim Brigade was there. Its general secretary is someone from Foca. Mustafa Oprasic, I know him well. He was sitting there in the office. I had had coffee with him on one occasion. He told me that Halid Cengic said -- had said bad things about me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification. You said you were sitting there in the office and you had coffee with him on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the motel --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: In the motel. Since he is from Foca and we knew each other from before the war. He worked in the forestry field. He had graduated from law school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know exactly what role he played in the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Well, he was the secretary. He kept all the records. He would register the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said the men took you to somewhere else and not to the Motel Sretno. Where did they take you to?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: They took me to the Music School in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain at the Music School in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during -- well, were you at the Music School -- did you remain there for seven days voluntarily or were you detained there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I was detained, and I was beaten so severely on the sixth day. My head was cracked. I lost consciousness for 24 hours. On the following day, when I woke up, covered in blood, Hodza was sitting next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't ask you what happened to you. It has been ruled that what happened to you is of no relevance here. So can you just listen to what I'm asking and answer it directly. While you were detained there for seven days, were there other prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone, because they interrogated me and took me to a room by the stairs, on my own. I was alone. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what you saw when they interrogated you.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA PODRUG
utterances.text: Well, I saw the bearded members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. They all had headbands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know wish to unnecessarily interrupt the witness, but he is now giving evidence about what happened to him during his interrogation. He has indicated that when he was there, various things happened to him, but he didn't see what happened to anyone else. And my learned friend is now asking him really what was happening to him, and I would ask that he shouldn't be allowed to give evidence about specifically his interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The record is that I asked him what he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Stamp. First of all, when he said that some things had happened to him, he said that spontaneously. No one was expecting him to say that, but he did. But then the Prosecution asked him what he had seen, what he had seen. Apparently, he was alone, but he must have seen other people, and he's been asked to say what he saw. He can say what he saw. He hasn't been asked to say what happened to him. He's been asked to say what he saw. There's a difference between something happening to you and seeing something. And in English, the word "see" is used. Mr. Stamp has asked him a question. There were certainly walls around him. There was a table. There were individuals there. Perhaps he could tell us what he saw around him. So, Mr. Stamp, please continue, and the Trial Chamber will pay attention to what's being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what you saw while you were being interrogated.
